title.en: How the World Began: Sky Woman's Fall and the Two Minds
title.zh: 世界之肇始：天女墜落與兩位心智

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin for Seneca oral tales)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（塞內卡口傳故事的採集定位）

texts.period: Recorded 1900s-1922 from Seneca informants on the Cattaraugus Reservation (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 1, 'How the World Began' (1923)

summary.en: In the sky world the Ancient One uproots the great tree at his dream's command and thrusts his pregnant wife through the hole; as she falls, the Fire Beast gives her corn, mortar, pot and pestle, and the water creatures receive her on the great turtle's back, where muskrat brings up earth. Her daughter dies giving birth to twins, and from her grave spring the beans, squash, corn and tobacco; Good Mind finishes the world, releases the animals from the bags of life, and seals his destructive brother Tawiskaron in the cave before molding the first men from clay.
summary.zh: 在天上世界中，遠古者依夢境之命連根拔起大樹，將懷孕的妻子推入洞中；她墜落時，火獸賜她玉米、臼、缽與杵，水中眾獸以巨龜之背承接她，麝鼠潛水取土。其女產下雙生而死，墓上生出豆、南瓜、玉米與菸草；善心者完成世界，自生命之袋釋出百獸，將其破壞之弟塔威斯卡隆封入洞穴，再以黏土捏塑最早的人類。

texts.language: Seneca oral tradition told in English

narrative.en:
Parker's fullest Seneca account of creation opens above the sky. Beyond the dome is another world, a floating land where the great chief and his celestial people live around a central tree of light whose roots run in four directions and whose luminous blossom fills the air with the perfume of burning tobacco. Dreaming, the Ancient One desires a maiden and marries her; she conceives from his potent breath, and his anger at finding her already with child drives the plot. Another dream commands him to uproot the celestial tree; his people try and fail, he uproots it himself, and leads his wife Iagen'tci (the Sky Woman) to peer into the hole. Pushed through it in rage, she snatches as she falls a handful of seeds and the tobacco leaf, and drops through the crust of the sky world.

Below is an unformed sea. As she falls, a fire-emitting beast named Gaa'siohdie't'ha' hands her a small pot, a corn mortar, a pestle, a marrow bone and an ear of corn, with the grim promise that all who eat will one day see him last of all. The water creatures, among them the spirits of Wind, the Defending Face, Thunder and Heavy Night, take council: ducks interlace their wings to receive her, the great turtle rises from below to offer his back, and muskrat alone touches bottom, smearing a little earth on the shell, which grows until it is an island world. The woman shakes out the seeds and sets the root she held, and a new tree of light rises over the turtle island.

Her daughter grows up swinging on a vine, laughs as if embraced, and bears twins, one kind and one warty and savage who tears his way out through his mother's side, killing her. From the daughter's grave, tended by Good Mind, sprout the stringed potato, beans, squash, corn and tobacco: the Three Sisters and the sacred plant grow out of a death. Grandmother Sky Woman then names the animals when Good Mind releases them from the bags of life his father gave him after his four-fold ordeal on the mountain of the east (he casts the cliff, swims the cataract, wrestles Wind and endures flame), and anoints the fat ones in a pool of oil. His jealous brother Tawiskaron (Evil Mind, Flint) follows behind, breeding thorns, poison plants and slimes, and twice attacks Good Mind with cat-tail flags and deer horns. Good Mind wins the final fight and banishes him to the cave with all the enchanted beasts, where he still gives orders. The whirlwind Great Defender is mastered with the mountain-moving test and his bent, twisted face becomes the likeness carved for the False Face Society; Thunder is engaged to slay whatever escapes the cave. At last Good Mind molds men and women of clay in his own image, teaches them hunting, fishing and the incense of tobacco, and departs up the sky road with the first beings.

The story is the anchor record of the Haudenosaunee cosmos: a matrilineal world built downward from a violated marriage and upward from a grave, with the twin polarity (Good Mind / Flint) that the Maya Hero Twins, the Navajo Changing-Bear Twins and countless dual-creator systems share. Its ritual harvest is enormous: corn as milk, tobacco as speech to the Creator, the False Face masks as Defender's contract, the cave as the residence of the Destroyer.

functions: Cosmogony: explains the earth as Turtle Island built by co-operative water beings
Agricultural charter: corn, beans, squash and tobacco grow from the murdered daughter's grave
Ritual charter: tobacco incense, False Face carving and Thunder's pest-control all contracted in the tale
Dualistic ethics: Good Mind finishes and beautifies, Flint spoils; sickness and mischief trace to the cave

texts.sensitivity_guidance: A central living-tradition narrative of the Haudenosaunee. Presented here from public-domain colonial-era transcriptions with respect; ceremonial details of False Face rituals are not disclosed.

sensitivity.note: Living Haudenosaunee tradition recorded 1900s-1922; published in Parker 1923 (public domain). Included as sacred narrative of record; not a ritual manual. Cross-tradition tagging of 'clay-humans' and 'sibling-creators' is an interpretive act (Thompson index is Euro-American).

passages.text: Beyond the dome we call the sky there is another world, a fair country where lived the great chief of the up-above-world and his celestial people. In the center of that world grew a great tree whose luminous blossom lighted the sky land, and whose roots ran in four directions. The Ancient One dreamed he must take as wife a certain fair maiden; when he found she was already with child he fell into a troubled sleep, and a dream commanded him to have the celestial tree uprooted as a punishment to his wife. She too found pleasure in the uprooting, wishing to know what was beneath it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 59-60; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief led his wife to the hole and seated her on its edge to peer downward; long she sat looking, until in rage he drew her blanket over her head and pushed her with his foot to thrust her into the hole. As she fell she gathered in her fingers all manner of seeds, and the tobacco leaf that grew from the broken root. Below, the creature-beings saw her coming and took council: the duck-creatures received her on their interknit wings, the great turtle made his back a resting-place, and muskrat alone touched the bottom and smeared earth upon the shell, whereupon the earth grew and the turtle grew with it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 61-62; not verbatim.

passages.text: In due season the Sky Woman bore a daughter, and the daughter, swinging on a vine as if embraced by a lover, bore twin boys. The words of one were kind, but the other, warty and savage, pierced his mother through the arm pit and stood upon her dead body. Where the daughter's feet were buried the stringed potato sprouted; from her fingers the beans; from her abdomen the squash; from her breasts the corn; and from her brow the tobacco. 'By these things we shall hereafter live,' said the grandmother, 'and the corn shall be your milk.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 63-64; not verbatim.

passages.text: After his father's ordeal by the mountain of the east, Good Mind opened the bags of life and the animals rushed forth. Twice his warty brother attacked him, first with cat-tail flags, then with deer horns, until Good Mind disarmed him and banished him to the mouth of the great cave with all the enchanted beasts, naming him Destroyer. The whirlwind Great Defender lost the mountain-moving test and his nose was bent and his mouth twisted forever - hence the carved faces that help the sick. Thunder promised to shoot whatever evil things escaped the under-world. Then Good Mind took clay, molded images of men and women, and when they were dry spoke to them and they sprang up and lived.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 67-73; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brothers Who Climbed to the Sky

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 2, 'The Brothers Who Climbed to the Sky' (1923)

summary.en: Three hunter brothers walk to the rim where sky meets sea. One is crushed beneath the falling dome but his spirit speeds ahead to the sky country; the two survivors are purified, dismembered and rebuilt by the Master of Life, watch a war on earth through a hole in the sky, and return aged to find fifty years gone - only to be killed at last by fiery shafts of the sky and barred from re-entry.
summary.zh: 三個獵人兄弟步行至天海相接之處。一人被落下的天穹壓碎，其靈卻先行抵達天界；倖存的兩人被生命之主淨化、拆解重組，從天上的孔洞俯瞰人間戰事，返鄉時已歷五十年，最後死於天空的火矛，再難重返。

sensitivity.note: Seneca folktale recorded by Parker 1923; public domain. Death-spirit etiquette (greeting first) is presented as story logic, not ritual instruction.

passages.text: Three brothers who had spent their lives as hunters resolved to walk to the end of the earth where the sky touches the water of the great seas. After many years they reached the spot where the blue dome bends down to earth; each day it rose high and fell back on the sea. Two brothers ran beneath the rim, and as they stepped out the farther side the wall came down and the third was crushed - but his spirit sped forward like the wind. On the other side of the sky all things seemed turned around, and a man came running toward them: it was their brother, who could only say, 'Never hesitate, never delay!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 74-75; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Father of All warned them: when you meet my son the Great Spirit, call him quickly 'Nya'we'skano', for if you fail to speak first he will say 'you are mine,' and you will be spirits. In the great white lodge the Master of Life laid one brother down, tapped his neck with a small shell, and skinned him - stripping every muscle, taking out the organs, cleansing each fibre with a fluid from his mouth, and putting him together again. Their bodies renewed, the brothers caught the Master's swiftest buck, and were led to a hill to look down through a hole in the sky at a war then raging on earth. 'Such things men will ever do,' said the Master of Life.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 75-76; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers lived long in the upper world and learned much that their tongues never could tell. At last they descended to earth by night and slept on the ground; in the morning their native village was overgrown with trees, and only one sister, aged, knew them - the war they had watched, they were told, took place fifty years ago. They did not love earth now but longed for their lodges in the sky world; neither pestilence nor enchantment could kill them, but two fiery shafts of the sky did. They journeyed back toward the great white lodge, but could not return, for the Creator had first spoken.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 77; not verbatim.

title.en: The Death Panther: Omen from the Under-Water World
title.zh: 死亡豹：水下世界之凶兆

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

texts.period: Recorded Jan. 1905, Edward Cornplanter informant, Cattaraugus (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 3, 'The Death Panther' (1923)

summary.en: Two boys dive in a mountain lake and one is led by a blue-skinned warrior into an under-water council where a preacher debates warning the earth of coming disasters. The boy keeps a forbidden lodge four moons, returns to find war, famine, pestilence and fire have swept his village, and learns that the blue panther floating in the trees with fire shooting from its tail is the herald of disaster - to be turned aside with burning tobacco.
summary.zh: 兩名少年在山間湖中潛水，其一被一位青色戰士引至水下議會，會中講道者正爭論是否該警示地上將臨之災。少年看守禁室四月，歸來時發現戰亂、饑荒、瘟疫與大火已毀其村，並得知那飄浮樹梢、尾噴火焰的青豹乃災禍之先兆——須以焚燒菸草化解。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Cornplanter informant, 1905), Parker 1923; public domain. The comet/fire-panther omen is a folk belief of record, not operative ritual.

passages.text: Two boys played in the waters of a deep lake beneath a tall white-headed mountain. Diving in contest, one boy, Oohoosha, clung to a flat rock and saw a tall warrior approach whose glistening body was the color of the sky. 'Come with me,' said the man, and Oohoosha strangely understood the unknown tongue. In a large moss-covered council hall under the water a stout preacher with a yellow and pink face was declaiming: 'The earth people are his children as well as we, so why should not we who know and foreknow many things notify them that trouble is coming?'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 78-79; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy's friend volunteered to go: 'It is my office.' He set out to warn the earth-world of disaster and left Oohoosha keeper of his lodge, forbidding him the back room. For four moons the boy kept watch; when the friend returned he sighed, 'Do not ask me. In my madness you may see me as I am. I am the messenger of death. I am in disguise, but should you see me you would soon die, so depart and preach what I whisper, that henceforth mankind may profit.' Oohoosha shot upward, found his clothing fresh beneath a rock, and went back to the village.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 79-80; not verbatim.

passages.text: The village was charred frames; a trail lined with dog bones led west to a few houses of gaunt, scarred survivors. His old comrade drew back with a cry: 'How came you back from death!' A devastating war, famine, pestilence and a marauding band's fire had swept them, and a warning sign had floated unheeded in the trees - a blue panther with no visible face, from whose tail shot flames of fire. 'That creature is the herald of disaster,' said Oohoosha. 'When he is seen all men must burn tobacco, for incense is the sign that disaster is not wanted; he will breathe it and turn aside the impending evil.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 80-81; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Bear Constellation: The Celestial Bear Chase

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin for the sky tale)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（此天空故事之採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 4, 'The Great Bear Constellation' (1923)

summary.en: Seven starving hunter brothers carry their 'lazy' brother in a litter; he secretly absorbs their strength and kills the great bear they have tracked into the sky. The bear's blood and oil stain the leaves red, orange and yellow - hence autumn - and the slain bear revives each year, so the chase of the hunter torch-bearers and the kettle-carrier circles the sky forever as the Big Dipper.
summary.zh: 七個飢餓的獵人兄弟以擔架抬著「懶惰」的弟弟；他暗中吸取眾兄之力，追蹤大熊上天並將其誅殺。熊血與油脂把樹葉染成紅、橙、黃——秋季由此而來——被殺的熊年年復生，於是持火把者與攜釜者的追逐繞天不息，是為北斗。

sensitivity.note: Seneca star legend (Parker 1923); public domain. Parallels the Micmac/Wabanaki celestial-bear chase of the same stars.

passages.text: In the days of the first people there were seven brothers, all hunters, but one was called the Lazy One. After many moons without game their hunger charged their minds with magic. Four brothers carried the reluctant one in a burden litter, one went before with a torch and one behind with a kettle. The leading brother saw the tracks of a large bear, and the lazy brother begged to be bathed with his brothers' salivary fluid, hoping to absorb their strength, and all paused to do it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 81; not verbatim.

passages.text: For three days more the bear tracks freshened ahead of them. At last the litter-bearers set the Lazy One down to help kill the bear - but he leaped up and ran ahead, full of power from the bath, and slew it with an axe. When they looked about they were far up in the air with the earth a good way below, and the blood and oil from the bear had stained the leaves of the trees red, orange and yellow. This is how the autumn leaves became colored.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 82-83; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon they found the bear had revived, though they had killed and eaten him, and being hungry they pursued and killed him again, and it was autumn again. This bear chase keeps up all the time, year after year, since the first people came. In the sky you may find the man with the torch at the end of the bear-chase cluster, and the man with the pot in the middle of the handle; the bear hides in a cave and comes out when the brothers are very hungry. So we call those stars Nia'gwai' hades'he' - Bear they pursuing are.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 83; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Brothers of the Star Cluster

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 5, 'The Seven Brothers of the Star Cluster' (1923)

summary.en: Seven warrior brothers dance themselves into the air with a magic song; forbidden to look down, the eldest cannot resist his mother's final plea and falls into the earth. From the scar grows the first pine, which only the weeping mother can interpret when it speaks; the other six become the dancing stars of the Pleiades and converse with their pine brother each winter.
summary.zh: 七個戰士兄弟以魔法之歌舞入空中；長兄雖被禁止低頭，卻敵不過母親最後的呼喚而墜入地中。傷口處長出第一棵松樹，唯有哭泣的母親能解其言語；其餘六人化為昂宿的舞星，每年冬天與松樹兄弟相語。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Parker notes the Huron/Wyandot parallel (Barbeau 1911).

passages.text: Seven brothers trained as young warriors practised daily before their mother's lodge while an uncle drummed on a water drum to teach them the dance. When they asked their mother for provisions for an expedition she scoffed and sent them away - once, twice, a third time. On the fourth dance the eldest changed his tune to the song of Djihaya, and with great enthusiasm sang, compelling his brothers to dance a dance of magic: the mother rushed out and saw her sons dancing in the air over the trees.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 83-84; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Heed no sounds from the earth but continue dancing,' called the eldest son, 'if you look down you shall fall and never more be able to dance.' But the mother gave a heart-broken cry - 'Oh my first born son, give your mother one last look or I die!' - and his heart weakened; he looked, lost his power to master the air, fell with great rapidity and penetrated the earth, leaving only a scar. The remaining boys became the dancing stars.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 84-85; not verbatim.

passages.text: For a whole year the mother wept beside the spot. In spring a tiny green shoot appeared, grew into a tall tree, and became the first pine; she guarded it, knowing it was her son. When a careless hunter slashed the tree, blood flowed, and the mother bound up the wound. In time the tree bore short feathers (cones) and more trees grew. Every winter the pine talked to its dancing brothers in the sky, and the mother knew that her eldest son should be her comfort while she rested on this earth.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 85; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Star Dancers: The Youth Who Married a Star

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 6, 'The Seven Star Dancers' (1923)

summary.en: A youth sent to dream by the river sees seven shining women dance on the water and descend in a corn basket. He seizes the youngest, is drawn up to the sky, is dismembered and regenerated by a great chief, and returns with his star bride - but so many years have passed that no one knows his uncle, and the couple, unable to live among men, go back up forever; the dimmest Pleiad is the wife who lost her brightness.
summary.zh: 青年奉命在河邊作夢，見七位發光女子在水上起舞、乘玉米籃降下。他捉住最年幼者，被引上天空，由大首領拆解重塑，攜星妻歸返人間——然而歲月已逝，無人識得他的叔父，二人無法與世人共處，終究重返天上；昂宿中最黯淡者便是失了光輝的妻子。

sensitivity.note: Seneca star-lore (Parker 1923); public domain. Parker cross-references Barbeau's Huron and Wyandot parallels.

passages.text: An uncle sent his nephew Djinae'nda to the river shore to dream until his dream-helpers appeared, fasting and sweating in the sweat lodge. One night he saw seven shining young women dancing in the water against the shore, going up and down without splashing; the youngest was the most beautiful. When he rushed out they leaped into a great corn basket and were drawn rapidly up into the sky. The next night he waited until she danced near, grasped her before she touched the basket, and was drawn upward as she fell in.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 86-87; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I want to marry you,' he said; 'you have caused me to love you.' 'Then we shall be married,' said the maiden, 'but we must return to the sky and prepare for living upon the earth.' A great chief of the sky caused him to recline, took him apart joint by joint, removed and cleansed all his organs, and replaced them: Djinae'nda was regenerated and felt strong enough for mighty things. Then the basket lowered the couple to the beach - but the river was changed and a great village stood there, and an old man said one such as his uncle had lived there more than a hundred years ago.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 87-88; not verbatim.

passages.text: The couple tried to live contentedly but could not understand the ways of the people; in time the two returned to the sky. The wife rejoined her sisters but had lost her brightness, and Djinae'nda roamed the sky world hunting game which he captured by running it down. My grandmother told me that they are up there yet.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 88; not verbatim.

title.en: The Coming of Spring: Winter's Lodge and the Young Warrior
title.zh: 春之來臨：冬神之屋與少年戰士

region.en: Shores of a great lake by a high mountain (symbolic pin at Lake Erie shore, New York)
region.zh: 大湖之濱、高山之下（象徵性定位於紐約州伊利湖岸）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 7, 'The Coming of Spring' (1923)

summary.en: An old man of frost builds a lodge of ice on a lake shore where every step freezes the ground; North Wind is his only guest, smoking with him and begging new tricks for burying villages. A smiling, glowing stranger - the Spring - breaks in his door, keeps on smoking, and sings until the old man shrinks to a whisper; an eagle carries him north, the ice breaks, rivers swell, and it is morning in spring time.
summary.zh: 冰霜老人在湖畔築冰屋，足跡所至大地堅如燧石；北風是他唯一的客人，與他共吸菸斗，並求取埋葬村莊的新詭計。一位含笑發光的陌生者——春——破門而入，不停吸菸，且歌且進，直至老人縮為一縷低語；老鷹將他攜往北方，冰河解凍，春之早晨來臨。

sensitivity.note: Seneca seasonal myth (Aurelia Miller informant, 1905), Parker 1923; public domain.

passages.text: An old man with long white flowing hair wandered over the land: where his footsteps fell the ground grew hard like flint, his breath made the leaves drop red, and rivers stood solid when he splashed through. On the shore of a great lake by a high mountain he built a lodge with walls of ice, guarded by uprooted stumps, and only his friend North Wind might enter and sit by the fire that gave flames but no heat. North Wind came chiefly for new tricks - how to pile the snow banks higher, cause famine, or make great snow-slides to bury Indian villages.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 88-89; not verbatim.

passages.text: One dismal night both fell asleep smoking; toward morning North Wind sprang up crying, 'What warm thing has bewitched me? The drifts are sinking, the rivers breaking, the ice is steaming!' A stranger stood striking the doorpost, and when the door fell he entered, hung it upright, and stirred the fire until it grew warmer. The old man raved, 'I am mighty! All snows and ice and frosts are my making... You do not belong in my lodge!' The stranger only smiled: 'I like to be sociable, let me stay a little longer and we will smoke together.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 89-90; not verbatim.

passages.text: Shaking with fear the old man drew smoke, and the warrior sang: 'I am Dedio's'wineq'dou, the Spring... My friend Daga'e'nda, the South Wind, is coming. I guess your friend is dead. There is a place. You cannot own all things always.' As he sang the old man shrank and shriveled until his voice only whispered, 'I don't know you!' A rushing wind shook the lodge, an eagle swooped down and carried the old man toward the north, and where the fire had burned a plant was growing. The swollen rivers carried away the ice, and in the morning it was spring time.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 90-91; not verbatim.

title.en: The Coming of Death: The Wise Man's Dream and the Nine Bands
title.zh: 死亡之來臨：智者之夢與九部議團

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. IV tale 8, 'The Coming of Death' (1923)

summary.en: In the newly made world people do not know death: men and children collapse breathless and are laid in tree limbs while everyone assumes such things happen only to others. One wise man dreams, and the Good Minded Spirit tells him the name of the faceless one who steals breath - Shondowekowa - and that every person will die. The wise man proclaims mortality to a council and organizes the people into nine caring bands, promising that the good will see the Maker's home when breath goes out of the body.
summary.zh: 在新造的世界中，人們尚不知死亡：男人孩童無息倒下，被安置於樹杈，人人皆以為此事只會降於他人。一位智者得夢，善心之靈告訴他那奪取氣息的無面者之名——舒恩多威科瓦——並說人人都必死。智者向議會宣告死之必然，並將人民編為九個互助議團，許諾行善者在氣息離體時將得見造物主之居所。

sensitivity.note: Seneca origin-of-death narrative (Parker 1923); public domain. Mortality here is announced, not caused by a broken taboo - a distinct Iroquoian variant of the world-wide 'origin of death' cluster.

passages.text: When the world was first made, men-beings did not know that they must die sometime. In those days a prominent man was found prone upon the grass, limp, without breath. He did not awaken, and when they placed him on his feet he fell like a tanned skin. A female man-being said he must be wrapped and put in the limbs of a tree; after a while the flesh dropped from the bones. Soon a child was found in the same condition, and laid in a tree also. Many others did these things, and no one knew why - no one thought that he himself would ever do such a thing.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 92; not verbatim.

passages.text: One wise man thought much about these things and had a dream: as he slept, the Good Minded Spirit came to him and spoke. Rising with a solemn face, he called the people together in council and said, 'A good word has come to me from the Good Minded spirit... They have died. It will be the same with all of you. The name of the one that steals away your breath is Shondowekowa. He has no face and does not see anyone; you cannot see him until he grasps you. He will continue to work forever. Every one who hears me and every one not yet born will die.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 92-93; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'You must now divide yourselves into nine bands, five to sit on one side of the fire and four on the other, and these bands shall care for their members. You must seek out all good things and instruct one another, and those who do good things will see the place where the Maker of all things lives when their breath goes out of their body.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 93; not verbatim.
